sections.heading: Daisugi Testnet v03 Launch
sections.summary: A primitive testnet v03 was launched on Daisugi with EIP-8288 and STARK-aggregated SPHINCS signatures; traffic generation tooling is still needed.
sections.body:
- Testnet v03 launched on Daisugi thanks to Gianluca and the Nethermind team, implementing a simple version of EIP-8288.
- One transaction demonstrated a STARK proof of 20 transaction signatures using a version of SPHINCS.
- Current main issue is lack of traffic; EthPandaOps tooling will be used to spam transactions for better benchmarks.
- A faster, more professionalized testnet is planned after Devcon.
- Next testnet upgrade will incorporate the Lean SPHINCS parameters agreed upon during this call, targeted within two weeks.

sections.heading: sphincs.art Parameter Explorer
sections.summary: Tom Wambsgans presented sphincs.art, a tool for exploring Lean SPHINCS parameter trade-offs including lifetime, tree shape, hash choice, and FTS type.
sections.body:
- sphincs.art is an opinionated web tool for understanding Lean SPHINCS parameter trade-offs, focusing on the biggest open questions.
- **Lifetime (signature budget):** Default is 2^30 (~1 billion signatures), conservative enough that typical users never worry about exhaustion; higher lifetime increases signature size and slows signing.
- **Tree shape:** Two options presented:
  - Uniform: vanilla SLH-DSA style with multiple small XMSS layers (e.g., 3 layers); KeyGen only needs the top layer, so it is fast.
  - Single large XMSS layer (similar to a recent NIST candidate): KeyGen is extremely slow without pruning.
- **Hash function:** Three options available (not elaborated in detail).
- **Few-time signature (FTS) type:**
  - FORS (vanilla, as in SLH-DSA): forest of random subsets.
  - Forest of small WOTS (novel, from Jonas Nick / Blockstream via sig.golf): uses 6 chains of height 5 per WOTS with a non-injective encoding that avoids grinding; roughly 30%+ better performance than comparable FORS.
    - Drawbacks: novel (needs new standard-model security analysis), higher variance in concrete security, and ~2× less MPC-friendly since nearly 100% of hashes are secret vs. ~50% in FORS.
- sphincs.art uses WOTS+C (not WOTS with checksum), making worst case equal to average case for permutation counts.
- The tool also shows threshold/MPC performance estimates, incorporating Revolabs/Project 11's idea of pre-generating FORS and delegating Ledger computation to a host via STARK proofs.

sections.heading: Pruning Trade-offs and Privacy
sections.summary: Pruning enables fast KeyGen on constrained devices but leaks privacy through FTS reuse; a semi-trusted state approach can provide ~2,000 private signatures on a Ledger.
sections.body:
- Pruning (developed by conduition) lets constrained devices like Ledger keygen only ~4,000 random FTS leaves instead of the full tree, filling the rest with surrogate nodes.
  - A broken link to the [conduition blog post on pruning](https://conduition.io/cryptography/hypertree-pruning/) was noted in chat.
- **Privacy concern:** With pruning, repeated signing eventually reuses the same FTS, allowing an observer to distinguish a pruned key and infer the subtree size.
  - Naive contiguous subtree selection is especially bad for privacy; randomly scattered subtree selection is possible with efficient surrogate algorithms.
  - With default pruning parameters, after ~75 signatures an adversary can distinguish with >50% advantage; for full privacy, signing should be limited to ~30 times.
- **Semi-trusted state mitigation:** If the signer tracks which FTS indices have been used and avoids reuse while the used set is ≤ half of available FTS:
  - Over 2,000 fully private signatures are achievable on a Ledger.
  - Cost: slightly more grinding at signing time.
  - If an adversary corrupts the state: cannot forge, but can leak subtree size and effectively halve the lifetime (e.g., from 100,000 to 50,000 signatures).
    - The adversary can claim unused FTS are used, forcing the signer onto the remaining half of the subtree.
  - Constraint: state must never exceed half of available FTS to bound adversary advantage to a factor of 2.
- Project 11's position: pruning should be optional, not the backbone of the scheme; users who understand the trade-offs can opt in.

sections.heading: Project 11 / Revolabs Parameter Proposals
sections.summary: Project 11 presented two SPHINCS parameter sets optimized for MPC and hardware wallets, both using FORS and CAIC, converging closely with sphincs.art's proposals.
sections.body:
- Project 11 (formerly Revolabs) focuses on constrained hardware (MPCs, hardware wallets) and older device compatibility.
- **SPHINCS-G:** A SPHINCS+ variant enabling 200–500 ms signing on constrained devices; paper expected next month.
- **Design principles:**
  - Signature size is not the top priority given aggregation is on the roadmap.
  - Aggregation friendliness is important but should not make the signature impractical, since SNARK improvements are rapid.
  - Signature budget should be large enough that non-specialized users never worry (≥ 2^20).
  - Stateful schemes are avoided; only stateless schemes considered.
  - FORS preferred over forest-of-WOTS for MPC: FORS allows ~50% of hashes to be public (not needing MPC), whereas WOTS requires MPC on nearly all hashes — a structural disadvantage not solvable by faster hardware.
  - CAIC chosen as hash function because it requires fewer MPC rounds.
- **Parameter set 1 (legacy/balanced):** Closer to SPHINCS+, balanced tree, bigger Winternitz parameter for smaller signatures, smaller FORS for MPC advantage, lifetime 2^24, size ~5.5 KB.
- **Parameter set 2 (Lean SPHINCS aligned):** Designed for compatibility with sphincs.art proposals; smaller FORS, dramatically reduced Winternitz parameter, lifetime 2^24, comparable size and permutation counts to sphincs.art.
- **Key design concept:** One single standard verification and aggregation process on Ethereum; hot wallets sign directly, constrained devices (MPC, Ledger) use SPHINCS-G or assisted signing while maintaining the same verifier — maximizing privacy for high-value custody setups.
- Project 11's research tool at research.project11.com will be expanded to support Lean SPHINCS variations.

sections.heading: WOTS+C vs. WOTS+ Clarification
sections.summary: Project 11 confirmed their tool still uses WOTS+ internally but they are evaluating WOTS+C for signature size savings; the switch is not yet finalized.
sections.body:
- Tom Wambsgans asked why Project 11's slides showed average vs. worst case if using WOTS+C (which makes them equal).
- Project 11 clarified: the tool still internally uses WOTS+ (with checksum), not WOTS+C; they computed numbers for the +C variant separately.
- WOTS+C is considered a small enough change from SPHINCS+ to be a good addition, but is not a hard requirement for Project 11.

sections.heading: Signature Lifetime Debate
sections.summary: Lifetime is the main unresolved parameter; proposals range from 2^24 to 2^30, with MPC/Ledger constraints favoring lower values and cross-ecosystem alignment favoring higher.
sections.body:
- Agreement that sphincs.art and Project 11 proposals are nearly identical except for lifetime (2^26–2^30 vs. 2^24).
- **Arguments for lower lifetime (2^24):**
  - Nico contacted 5 major exchanges (biggest active nonces on Ethereum); all said key rotation was not a problem — automated scripts, rotation takes <0.5 seconds.
  - On-chain data shows no accounts with billions of signatures even without rotation requirements.
  - Frame transactions can bundle operations, reducing per-day signature counts.
  - Project 11: going from 2^24 to 2^32 at the MPC layer is a "make-or-break" difference; higher H means worse grinding on Ledger devices.
  - Matteo Vena: if rotation infrastructure must be built anyway, the difference between 2^24 and 2^28 is marginal for the user but costly for constrained devices.
- **Arguments for higher lifetime (2^30):**
  - Justin Drake: easier to go from big to small than vice versa; a billion signatures is easy to communicate; alignment with Bitcoin (currently at 2^40, might go to 2^30; 2^24 may be a hard sell for conservative Bitcoiners).
  - Antonio Sanso: Circle's 30K–70K daily hot wallet signatures (~2^17/day) suggest conservatism.
  - Cognitive simplicity of a very large number reduces user/developer friction.
- **Circle (Daniel Cason):** Signs 30,000–70,000 transactions per day with hot wallets; needs to confirm internally whether rotation is problematic; prefers not rotating often; would like stateless SPHINCS+ verification as a precompile (pure function).
  - Antonio Sanso clarified: no precompile is planned because individual SPHINCS signatures are not verified on-chain; only the ZK proof of aggregated signatures is verified.
  - Circle to report back next meeting with more details on their rotation constraints.
- **Bitcoin alignment:** SHRINCS (Bitcoin proposal) uses 2^40 lifetime partly to cover off-chain protocols like high-volume Lightning nodes. Justin Drake suggested a three-way discussion (Ethereum, Bitcoin, MPC providers) to converge on lifetime.
- Nico: anything above 2^22 or 2^23 is more than enough based on user research.

sections.heading: Agreed Next Steps and Open Items
sections.summary: Consensus to adopt sphincs.art parameters for the next testnet upgrade; lifetime remains the only open question, to be resolved offline before the next call.
sections.body:
- Agreement: sphincs.art version 2 parameters (FORS-based, WOTS+C) will be used for the next testnet upgrade, as they are nearly identical to Project 11's aligned proposal.
- No objections to this approach.
- **Open item:** Lifetime parameter still undecided; to be resolved offline.
  - Antonio Sanso initially proposed starting with a high lifetime (2^30–2^32) to be conservative, but several participants argued for 2^24–2^26.
  - Tom Wambsgans agreed to add a 2^24 toggle to sphincs.art for comparison.
- Circle (Daniel Cason) to investigate key rotation feasibility internally and report back at the next meeting.
- Testnet update with new parameters targeted within two weeks.
- Next call in two weeks.

sections.heading: Grinding Constraints on Ledger vs. MPC
sections.summary: Ledger grinding is the binding constraint for higher H values; MPC grinding is manageable, and SNARK-assisted grinding for hardware wallets will improve ~10× within 12 months.
sections.body:
- Increasing H (tree height) requires more grinding; this is fine on laptop CPUs and in MPC but painful on Ledger hardware.
  - MPC does not need anti-steering proofs, so it runs faster.
  - Ledger needs both grinding and an anti-steering proof, making it the bottleneck.
- Justin Drake: hardware wallet grinding will improve ~10× over the next 12 months due to SNARK technology advances.
  - Two approaches for hardware wallet grinding: internal (slow, limited by hardware) or host-assisted with a SNARK proof of grinding to prevent cheating.
  - Larger proofs of grinding will become feasible as SNARKs improve.
- Nico: at a 2^26 lifetime (sphincs.art, uniform) signing takes ~24 seconds; at 2^30 it rises to ~40 seconds.
- Project 11 confirmed that H up to 2^24 is manageable for Ledger; going to 2^26–2^28 for MPC is "a bit slower but fine."
